title: Jaap close
hookLine: the Tenth Guru's praise now sits beside Nanak's Japji in your morning

lines: A MORNING YOU'D KNOW IN THE DARK.
THEN A FASTER ONE WITH A DRUMBEAT.
cards: Some mornings have a shape you'd recognize in the dark. Feet on the cold floor. Water on the face.
The kettle, the same mug. In Sikh homes that keep Nitnem, the shape has words too, in a fixed order. First a quiet, thoughtful voice, the first Guru's.
Then a faster one, written generations later, with a drumbeat in it. Thirty days ago you only knew the first.

teach.h: JAPJI OPENS ONE GRANTH, JAAP THE OTHER.
teach.b: Put the two side by side.

teach.h: THE FIRST GURU, THEN THE TENTH.
teach.b: Japji is Guru Nanak's, the first Guru, and it opens the Guru Granth Sahib on page one. Jaap is Guru Gobind Singh's, the tenth Guru, and it opens the Dasam Granth. Two first pages, two Gurus many generations apart.

Japji begins with Ik Onkar, One, and the Mool Mantar: true Name, creator, without fear, without hatred, timeless, unborn. Jaap begins with no mark, no caste, then salutes the One as akaal, abhai, ajooni.
Same truths, different walk. Japji thinks its way forward, pauri by pauri, asking questions. Jaap marches, name after name, through many meters and languages.
Sikhs believe the same light, the same jot, passed from Guru Nanak to each Guru in turn.

teach.h: ONE LIGHT, ONE JOT, IN BOTH.
teach.b: Saying Japji and then Jaap each morning is a small way of hearing that: the first Guru's voice, then the tenth, and the light in both. Now look back at the road. The morning praise, Jaap Sahib.
No mark, no caste. King of kings. Named by deeds.
The snake's gait. Akaal, the Timeless. The Merciful.
Formless, beyond compare. Ajooni, unborn. The armed One, the protector.
Sun of suns. Song of songs. The lamp of beauty.
The provider. Gobind. One form, many sights.
Ender and sustainer. Karunaa, the house of compassion. Breaker of the cruel.
The one-letter meter. Abhai. Every land.
Beyond the fear of death. Keeping the pace. The last stanza.
The whole Jaap. Tomorrow, the third morning bani: ten verses under the heading by your grace.

how: In the Sikh morning Nitnem, Japji Sahib is recited first and Jaap Sahib second, followed by the Tav Prasad Savaiye; many Sikhs say all three before or around dawn.

o: a pilgrimage to the gurdwaras of Punjab
the daily round of set prayers, in order
a yearly fast kept before a festival

games.q: Japji and Jaap — tap the pairs.
p: Guru Gobind Singh, the tenth Guru
page one of the Guru Granth Sahib
the one light passed from Guru to Guru

s: Japji and Jaap open the same book
Japji opens the Guru Granth Sahib; Jaap opens the Dasam Granth.
in the morning Nitnem, Japji comes before Jaap
the first Guru's voice, then the tenth.
Japji and Jaap teach unrelated ideas
the same truths, timeless, fearless, unborn, in a different walk.

games.q: it's morning and you have two banis to say: Guru Nanak's Japji and the Tenth Guru's Jaap. in what order do Sikhs say them?
games.why: the Rehat Maryada lists Japji, then Jaap, then the Tav Prasad Savaiye: the first Guru's voice, then the tenth.

practice: Picture tomorrow morning: where you'll be, what you'll do first, and the place where a few lines of Jaap could go.
A recording while you dress, the four words ajai, alai, abhai, abai at the window, or the full fifteen minutes if your life allows. Choose one, gently, and rest.

wordCard.voice: Nitnem, the daily rule of prayer. After thirty days, the Tenth Guru's morning praise sits beside Guru Nanak's Japji: the first Guru's voice, then the tenth.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: nitnem, the daily rule of prayer, in which Japji comes first and Jaap second.

carryVoice: Your line: japji, then jaap. One light, heard in both voices each morning. Jaap, done.

sources.ref: Sikh Rehat Maryada, Nitnem (Japji, Jaap, Tav Prasad Savaiye)
Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1 (Mool Mantar and Japji)
